The JK flip-flop is the most widely used flip-flop. It is part of many digital circuits.
INTRODUCTIONM
It can perform the functions of a RS, Clocked RS and Type D

LESSON MENU
1. JK FLIP-FLOPSTLE
The JK flip-flop is designed to store the last input condition until the next input condition is applied.
DISCUSSION
JK flip-flops have five inputs and two outputs.
The C input below represents the clock input. Some other common designations for the clock input include CLK, CK,

SYNCHRONOUS - Having a fixed time relationship. The output of a device changes state only at a specified point on a triggering input, such as a clock signal.
DEFINITION
Inputs J and K determine the operating characteristics of the flip-flop. Let's use the JK flip-flop as an RS flip-flop.
A low applied to the J and K inputs disables the clock input.
The flip-flop stays in its current state.
Applying a low to PRE and a high to CLR sets Q high and Q low.
Applying a high to PRE and a low to CLR sets Q high and Q low.
When J and K are low, PRE and CLR operate like the R and S inputs to an RS flip-flop.
Next, let's use the JK flip-flop as a Clocked RS flip-flop.
A high applied to PRE and CLR disables these inputs........
A high applied to the J input and a low applied to the K input sets Q high and Q low when the clock is high.
A low applied to the J input and a high applied to the K input sets Q high and Q low when the clock is high.
When J and K have opposite inputs, J and K operate like the R and S inputs to a Clocked RS flip-flop.
Next, let's use a JK flip-flop as a Type D flip-flop.......
Only one input to the flip-flop is needed. DATA is sent to J and inverted and sent to K.
DATA is applied to the flip-flop. Input J receives a high and input K receives a low on a high clock.
A low DATA input will place a low on Q and a high on Q when the clock is high.
Adding an inverter to the K input causes the J input to operate like the D input to a Type D flip-flop.
Remember, the JK flip-flop operates like an RS, Clocked RS or Type D flip-flop depending on the J and K inputs.
Highs on J and K are not an illegal state for the JK flip-flop.
A high on J and K sets the flip-flop to the toggle state.
On each clock pulse, the state of the flip-flop changes or toggles.
What is the output state of this flip-flop?
With lows on J and K, the flip-flop operates like a RS. A low on PRE or CLR sets or resets the flip-flop.

This JK flip-flop is constructed from four NAND gates with three inputs each. JK flip-flops are also constructed from NOR gates.
Note, the JK flip-flop applies feedback from gates C and D to gates A and B.
Note, the JK flip-flop applies feedback from gates C and D to gates A and B.
Also, the JK flip-flop adds an additional input to gates C and D.
Three input NAND gates require all three inputs be high to produce a low output. Any low input produces a high output.
Three input NAND gates require all three inputs be high to produce a low output. Any low input produces a high output.
Definition
Any low to the input of gate C sets the flip-flop.
Any low to the input of gate D resets the flip-flop.
To use the JK flip-flop as a RS flip-flop the J and K inputs must be low producing a high output on gates A and B.
PRE and CLR inputs are normally high. The output of the flip-flop is held in the last known state by the feedback between gates C and D.
A low input from CLR to gate D resets the flip-flop.
A low input from PRE to gate C sets the flip-flop.
With high outputs from gates A and B, the PRE and CLR inputs act like S and R inputs to a RS flip-flop.
Using the JK flip-flop as a Clocked RS flip-flop the PRE and CLR inputs must be high. The J and K inputs are used to set or reset the flip-flop when the clock is high.
When set, gate A has a low feedback signal from gate D. The feedback keeps the output of gate A high.
Gate B has a high feedback signal from gate C. If inputs K or C are low, the output of gate B is high.
When K and C are high, all three inputs to gate B are high.
The output goes low and resets the flip-flop.
When K and C are high, all three inputs to gate B are high.
The output goes low and resets the flip-flop.
If a high is applied to inputs J and C, the flip-flop changes state from reset to set.
If a high is applied to inputs J and C, the flip-flop changes state from reset to set.
To use the JK flip-flop as a type D flip-flop only requires the addition of an inverter between the J and K inputs.
In the toggle state of the JK flip-flop, highs are applied to J and K.
When the clock input goes high, the output of the flip-flop will change states.
With the flip-flop set, gate B produces a low output resetting the flip-flop.
With the flip-flop set, gate B produces a low output resetting the flip-flop.
With the flip-flop reset, gate A produces a low output setting the flip-flop.
With the flip-flop reset, gate A produces a low output setting the flip-flop.
Remember, the J and K inputs determine the type of flip-flop.
What is the output state of this flip-flop?
With lows on J and K, the flip-flop functions as a RS flip-flop. Look at the PRE and CLR inputs.

How is this JK flip-flop being used?
With J and K low, the clock is disabled. The PRE and CLR inputs are used to set or reset the flip-flop.

How is this JK flip-flop being used?
With highs on J and K, the flip-flop changes state on each clock pulse.

The JK flip-flop is more commonly constructed as a edge triggered device instead of a level triggered device.
The positive edge triggered flip-flop synchronously transfers data to the output only on a positive going transition (PGT) of the clock input.
Note from the timing diagram below that the output ONLY changes on the positive going transition and not during the high state of the clock signal.

The JK flip-flop can also have an active low clock. In this case the output will only change on a negative going transition (NGT) of the clock input.

In addition to the synchronous inputs the JK flip-flop may also have 1 or 2 asynchronous inputs.
These inputs cause the output to change regardless of the state of the clock or other synchronous inputs. When in their active state the asynchronous inputs cause the output to SET or RESET.
The operation of the asynchronous inputs can be expressed in a truth table.
While the asynchronous inputs have no standard designation there are several common designations given below:
PRESET (PRE)
CLEAR (CLR)
CD (DIRECT CLEAR)
